new.title: Lie back under the dome at the Mediendom
new.desc: On the HAW Kiel campus in Dietrichsdorf, the Mediendom is a 360 degree dome theatre that doubles as a planetarium. Its 64 seats sit in rings under the dome, and it hosts around 1,400 shows a year, from star talks to full-dome music shows.
new.tip: Book online, as the small hall sells out on weekends. The university observatory next door runs occasional public observing evenings that start at the Mediendom entrance.

new.title: Go inside the Flandernbunker at Kiel-Wik
new.desc: This naval high bunker by the Wik military harbour was built in 1943 and 1944, with walls 2.5 metres thick and a 4 metre roof. It sheltered up to 750 submarine crew and served as a radio and command centre; today the Mahnmal Kilian association runs it as a museum and place of remembrance.
new.tip: Check the association's website for guided tours and exhibition openings, which are often on Sunday afternoons. Combine it with a walk along the northern Kiellinie.

new.title: Find the canal's foundation stone at Holtenau lighthouse
new.desc: The brick lighthouse at the end of the Tiessenkai has guided ships into the Kiel Canal since the day the canal opened in 1895. The foundation stone and founding charter of the canal are set into its base, and its octagonal lower hall is used as a wedding room.
new.tip: The tower is only open on guided tours, but the lawn at its foot is the best free seat for watching ships enter the locks and the fjord.

new.title: Climb to the pavilion in the Old Botanical Garden
new.desc: Laid out as an English landscape park in 1825 and turned into a botanical garden by Adolf Engler by 1884, this hilly 2.5 hectare garden in Düsternbrook was the first in the world planted by plant geography. Look for a huge ginkgo, two dawn redwoods and an octagonal brick pavilion from 1891 with views over the fjord.
new.tip: Come in spring when the slopes are covered in bulbs. The half-timbered inspector's house is now the Literaturhaus, which holds readings.
new.q: Alter Botanischer Garten, Düsternbrooker Weg, Kiel

new.title: Eat North German food above the canal at Margaretental
new.desc: This country restaurant in Suchsdorf sits on a slope right above the Kiel Canal, and nearly every seat on its veranda and in the Lotsenzimmer looks out over the water. The kitchen cooks traditional northern dishes with produce from local farms, reviving some forgotten recipes along the way.
new.tip: Reserve a veranda table for late afternoon and watch freighters glide past at eye level. The covered terrace works even on breezy days.

new.title: Have vegan cake at Prinz Willy
new.desc: A small café and coworking space on Lutherstraße near the Schrevenpark, Prinz Willy is a fixture of Kiel's student quarter. Afternoons bring waffles and vegan cakes, and evenings regularly turn into concerts and other events.
new.tip: It keeps short afternoon hours, so check the website before you go and look for evening gigs.

new.title: Have lunch over the fjord at the Seebar
new.desc: The Seebar stands on the historic sea bathing pier of Düsternbrook, right on the water of the Kiel Fjord. It serves burgers, bowls and cocktails with ferries and sailing ships passing just metres away.
new.tip: From mid June to mid September the bathing area next door is open, so bring a towel and swim before you eat. The bar is closed on Mondays and Tuesdays.

new.title: Eat cheap and veggie at the Subrosa in Gaarden
new.desc: Run as a collective since 1995, the Subrosa is a café, pub and kitchen in the heart of multicultural Gaarden on the east shore. The food is vegetarian and vegan and kindly priced, and there is a cultural programme on top.
new.tip: Walk over the Hörnbrücke from the main station; it is about ten minutes on foot from there.

new.title: Feed the deer in the Projensdorfer Gehölz
new.desc: This 200 hectare forest by the Kiel Canal was planted around 1900 on the earth dug out for the canal. Inside lies the Tiergehege Tannenberg, at about 40 hectares the largest animal park run by the city, with deer and other native animals free to visit.
new.tip: Climb the 37 metre Tannenberg, then loop back past the Erlenkampsee. It is a favourite Sunday walk for local families.

new.title: Wake Asmus Bremer at the Kieler Umschlag
new.desc: First recorded in 1469, the Umschlag was a medieval money and trade fair, revived as a folk festival in 1975. On the last weekend of February crowds make noise to wake the figures of mayor Asmus Bremer and his wife, the mayor's trousers are hoisted on St. Nikolai, and pirates roam the Holstenstraße and the Alter Markt.
new.tip: Be at the Warleberger Hof on Thursday evening for the noisy opening procession. On Sunday the couple are put back to bed there, which closes the festival.

new.title: Roar with the crowd at a THW Kiel handball game
new.desc: THW Kiel is Germany's record handball champion, and home games fill the Ostseehalle in the city centre. The hall itself opened for Kieler Woche in 1951, built quickly from parts of old aircraft hangars brought over from Sylt.
new.tip: Tickets for big games go fast, so buy them online well ahead. The crowd sings from the first whistle, so expect to lose your voice.

new.title: Cycle along the Kiel Canal from Holtenau
new.desc: The Kiel Canal opened in 1895 and runs almost 100 km from Holtenau to Brunsbüttel on the Elbe. Paths along its banks let walkers and cyclists ride beside container ships that seem to slide through the fields.
new.tip: Start at the Holtenau end and ride west towards the Levensau bridges. Free canal ferries along the way let you switch banks.

new.title: Eat a fish roll at Fischhaus Loof on Husum harbour
new.desc: Right on the inner harbour of Husum, Fischhaus Loof sells smoked fish, matjes, herring and its own North Sea shrimp, the Loof-Krabben. Locals sit outside with fish rolls in summer.
new.tip: Ask for a shrimp roll made with freshly peeled Krabben. The counter also sells smoked fish to take home.

new.title: Taste salt marsh lamb at the Lammkontor in Husum
new.desc: The Nordfriesisches Lammkontor raises its own lamb on the salt marshes outside the dikes, plus Galloway and Limousin beef from the marshes. Its restaurant, farm shop and Deichbar sit together on Deichstraße in Husum.
new.tip: Salzwiesenlamm is in season from April to December. The restaurant takes a winter break until the end of February, but the farm shop stays open.

new.title: Dine among the shells at Kolles Alter Muschelsaal
new.desc: The Kolle family has run this restaurant on Büsum's harbour street for about 100 years, now in the fourth generation. Its dining room, the Muschelsaal, is known for its striking shell decoration.
new.tip: It is closed on Mondays and opens only in the evening on Tuesdays. Walk across to the harbour afterwards to see the shrimp cutters come in.

new.title: Raise a dram at the Blaue Maus on Amrum
new.desc: This island bar in Wittdün is a cult stop for whisky lovers, with its own cask bottlings and island spirits such as Amrumer Rum. It is a cosy place to end a windy day on Amrum.
new.tip: It opens only Friday to Monday from 6 pm and does not take reservations, so come early in high season.

new.title: Join the islanders at Glaube-Liebe-Hoffnung in Wyk
new.desc: A classic harbour and sailors' pub in Wyk auf Föhr, decorated with seafaring trophies and stuffed animals from around the world. Islanders and holidaymakers share the bar over Flensburger beer, Manhattans and wine, and it is open all year.
new.tip: Evenings are the time to go. On Bundesliga days it opens early for the match.

new.title: Eat smoked fish at Brauer's Aalkate on the canal
new.desc: In Rade, between Kiel and Rendsburg, the Brauer family's eel cottage sits right on the Kiel Canal. They catch their own fish, including eel in season, smoke it in their own smokehouse and serve it on a terrace where ships pass by.
new.tip: The restaurant opens only on Fridays and Sundays and on event days; the little fish shop opens on Thursdays.

new.title: Drink a Borbyer Bock with a bay view in Eckernförde
new.desc: Land in Sicht is a brewpub above Eckernförde Bay that brews its own Borbyer Bock and Eckernförder Pils and pours around 20 beers on tap. Every seat looks out over the water.
new.tip: Weekdays it opens at 4 pm, weekends at noon. It closes for a winter break in January.
new.q: Land in Sicht, Am Exer 1, Eckernförde

new.title: Take coffee and cake by the Schwentine in Preetz
new.desc: The Preetzer Cafestuben in the old town has a romantic garden that runs down to the Schwentine river. It serves breakfast, lunch and homemade cake, and guests can even arrive by boat.
new.tip: Closed on Mondays. Combine it with a visit to Preetz convent a few minutes' walk away.

new.title: Sip a sundowner on stilts in the Schlei at Kappeln
new.desc: The Seagull harbour bistro is built on piles right in the Schlei, surrounded by the yachts of Kappeln's southern marina. Its terrace is the place for local beer, wine and a simple meal over the water.
new.tip: Open Friday to Tuesday from 2 pm. Book ahead for the monthly Sunday brunch.

new.title: Smell the beans at the Sylt coffee roastery in Rantum
new.desc: The Kaffeerösterei Sylt roasts its own blends with island names like Flut, Ebbe and Fofftig-Fofftig, and serves them in its café on Hafenstraße in Rantum, on the Wadden Sea side of the island.
new.tip: Open daily from 11 am. A bag of beans makes a souvenir that actually tastes of the trip.

new.title: Eat in a merchant's courtyard at the Roter Hof
new.desc: Off Flensburg's Rote Straße, lined with old merchant courtyards, the Roter Hof restaurant fills one of the prettiest of them. It serves homemade cake and Viennese coffee by day and burgers and currywurst in the evening.
new.tip: Closed on Sundays. Sit outside in the courtyard on a sunny day.

new.title: Walk through old farmhouses at the Molfsee open-air museum
new.desc: Just outside Kiel, the Freilichtmuseum Molfsee is the largest open-air museum in northern Germany. More than 70 historic buildings from across Schleswig-Holstein stand on 40 hectares, and the modern Jahr100Haus covers everyday life in the 20th century.
new.tip: Open Tuesday to Sunday. Allow at least half a day, as the grounds are large.

new.title: See the nuns' choir stalls at Preetz Convent
new.desc: Founded in 1211 or 1212, the Benedictine convent of Preetz became a foundation for noblewomen after the Reformation and still is one today. Its Gothic church, built around 1320 to 1335, keeps carved choir stalls from about 1330 that once seated 70 nuns, plus a Renaissance organ from 1573.
new.tip: The convent grounds with their scattered ladies' houses are lovely to walk through. Check the convent's website for church opening times and tours.

new.title: Walk through Emil Nolde's garden at Seebüll
new.desc: Painter Emil Nolde and his wife Ada built their flat-roofed brick house on a lonely mound near the Danish border from 1927. After his death it became a museum of his work, surrounded by the flower garden the couple planted with old perennials and apple trees.
new.tip: The museum closes for the winter and reopens in March. Come in late summer when the garden is at its most colourful.

new.title: Walk across the Eider storm surge barrier
new.desc: Opened in 1973 at the mouth of the Eider near Tönning, the Eidersperrwerk is Germany's largest coastal protection structure. Its gates close against North Sea storm surges, and a road runs over the top.
new.tip: Watch the gates and the lock from the dike, then look out over the Wadden Sea on the seaward side. It is a short drive from the Multimar in Tönning.

new.title: Climb the 295 steps of Amrum's lighthouse
new.desc: Standing on a 25 metre dune in the south of the island, the Amrum lighthouse has shone since 1875. At 41.8 metres it is the tallest lighthouse you can climb on Germany's North Sea coast, and its light reaches 23 nautical miles.
new.tip: Visits are by guided tour in the summer half of the year. On a clear day the view takes in Föhr, Sylt and the Halligen.

new.title: Visit St. Severin, Keitum's church on the hill
new.desc: The 33 metre tower of St. Severin stands apart from the village on the highest point of Sylt's old geest core. The church is first mentioned in 1240, and its roof timbers date from 1216.
new.tip: Walk out from Keitum's thatched lanes and wander the churchyard, where old gravestones tell the stories of Sylt sea captains.

new.title: Watch the seal pups at Friedrichskoog
new.desc: Since 1985 the Seehundstation Friedrichskoog has been the only authorised rescue centre for orphaned seals in Schleswig-Holstein, raising more than 200 pups a year before releasing them. Resident harbour seals and grey seals can be watched from land and through underwater windows.
new.tip: Time your visit for a feeding: the resident seals are fed at 10:30 and 14:00. Summer is pup season.
new.q: Seehundstation Friedrichskoog, An der Seeschleuse 4, Friedrichskoog

new.title: Stand on Germany's largest market square in Heide
new.desc: At 4.7 hectares, the Marktplatz in Heide is the largest open market square in Germany. It began in the 15th century as the meeting place of the farmers' republic of Dithmarschen.
new.tip: Come on market day to see it busy, then step into St. Jürgen church on the square.

new.title: Explore the Museumsberg above Flensburg
new.desc: On a hill above the theatre, two buildings make up one of the largest museums in Schleswig-Holstein, covering art and culture of the Schleswig region from the 13th to the 20th century. The collection began in 1876 with furniture maker Heinrich Sauermann's antiques.
new.tip: Walk through the Alter Friedhof and the Christiansenpark next door afterwards; both belong to the same green hilltop.

new.title: See the ruined tower of Pellworm's Old Church
new.desc: Built around 1200, the Alte Kirche St. Salvator stands in the far west of Pellworm, and its broken tower ruin is the island's landmark. Legend says the pirate Cord Widderich used the tower as a base around 1400.
new.tip: Rent a bike at the harbour and ride across the island; the flat marsh makes the tower visible from far away.

new.title: See Tönning's old Packhaus on the harbour
new.desc: Built in 1783, the Packhaus on Tönning's harbour recalls the town's trading past and once appeared on a German postage stamp. It holds a town history exhibition, markets and events, and in December it is lit up as a giant Advent calendar.
new.tip: On several Wednesday evenings in summer you can watch locals peel North Sea shrimp here and learn the knack yourself, for free.

new.title: Climb the Bülk lighthouse at the mouth of the fjord
new.desc: Finished in 1865, Bülk lighthouse on the north shore near Strande is the oldest lighthouse on the Kiel Fjord. Its viewing platform is open to visitors and looks over the fjord entrance and the Stollergrund shoal.
new.tip: Walk or cycle there along the coast from Strande. Big ferries to Scandinavia pass close by on their way into Kiel.

new.title: Hike along the Morsum-Kliff on Sylt
new.desc: In the quiet east of Sylt, the Morsum-Kliff runs for nearly 2 km. Ice age glaciers pushed and tilted its layers, so red, white and black sands millions of years old now lie side by side; it is a nature reserve and a national geotope.
new.tip: Follow the marked path along the top and loop back by the beach. It is far less crowded than the west coast.

new.title: Walk to Germany's northern tip on the Ellenbogen
new.desc: North of List, the Ellenbogen peninsula curls into the North Sea with two lighthouses and empty beaches. Near List West lies the northernmost point of Germany, with the Danish island of Rømø just across the water.
new.tip: The road is private: cars pay a toll, but walkers and cyclists go free. Do not swim here, as currents along the north and east shores are dangerous.

new.title: Ride the Angeln steam train from Kappeln
new.desc: The Angelner Dampfeisenbahn is a volunteer-run museum railway between Kappeln on the Schlei and Süderbrarup, using mostly Scandinavian engines and carriages. It puffs through the rolling farmland of Angeln.
new.tip: Trains run on set days from Easter into autumn; book seats online at least 18 hours ahead. You can combine the trip with a boat on the Schlei.

new.title: Sail the Flensburg Fjord on the steamer Alexandra
new.desc: Launched in 1908, the Alexandra is the last surviving fjord steamer and a listed historic ship. Volunteers keep her running, and in summer she takes passengers out from Flensburg's historic harbour.
new.tip: The season starts in May. Reserve by phone or email; leftover tickets go on sale at the pier 30 minutes before departure.

new.title: Swim in the clear Ihlsee at Bad Segeberg
new.desc: On the edge of Bad Segeberg, the Ihlsee is one of the few nutrient poor lakes in Schleswig-Holstein, fed only by groundwater and rain, which keeps it unusually clear. It lies in a nature reserve with a long-standing bathing spot on the east shore.
new.tip: Go early on hot days, as the bathing area fills up. Out of season the walk around the lake is lovely too.

new.title: Cycle out to the Hamburger Hallig
new.desc: A causeway built in the 1860s crosses the salt marsh to this half island off the Reußenköge, about 4 km beyond the sea dike. The area has been a nature reserve since 1930 to protect avocets, and the Hallig Krog inn on the main mound serves visitors from Easter to October.
new.tip: Cars are limited, so bike or walk the causeway and watch for wading birds. Bring a windproof jacket; there is no shelter on the way.

new.title: Stroll through Arnis, Germany's smallest town
new.desc: With fewer than 300 people on 0.45 square kilometres, Arnis on a Schlei peninsula is the smallest town in Germany. It was founded in 1667 by 65 families from Kappeln escaping serfdom, and its one long street leads to a sailors' church with votive ships hanging from the ceiling.
new.tip: Walk the whole street to the church and back along the water. In the churchyard, QR codes beside some gravestones let you listen to the stories of local families.

new.title: Meet the bison at the Tierpark Neumünster
new.desc: In 24 hectares of woodland, the Tierpark Neumünster keeps around 700 animals of 100 species and is known for breeding European bison, some of which have been released in the Romanian Carpathians. It also has a rebuilt Nissen hut and a geest farmhouse.
new.tip: Pair it with a walk in the town forest right next door.

new.title: Follow the boardwalk to Amrum's little lighthouse
new.desc: From the woods near Norddorf a boardwalk of about 1.4 km winds through wild dunes to a small range light, the Kleiner Leuchtturm. It is one of Amrum's best viewpoints over the Kniepsand.
new.tip: Leave your bike at the racks by the Vogelkoje. Keep going over the sand to the waterline for the full North Sea feeling.
